glossary.Hypersensitivity: An exaggerated immune response to a harmless substance that damages the body's own tissues.
glossary.Reversible obstruction: Narrowing of the airways that improves, either by itself or with a bronchodilator.
glossary.Eczema: An itchy, dry, inflamed skin condition, often part of atopy.
glossary.Hay fever: Allergic rhinitis: sneezing, runny nose and itchy eyes triggered by pollen.
glossary.Allergen: A normally harmless substance, such as pollen or cat dander, that triggers an allergic reaction.
glossary.Wheeze: A high-pitched whistling sound, mainly on breathing out, caused by narrowed airways.
glossary.Prolonged expiration: Breathing out taking longer than normal because air leaves narrowed airways slowly.
glossary.Rescue medication: A reliever inhaler, usually salbutamol, used to ease symptoms during an attack.
glossary.Exacerbation: A flare-up where symptoms get worse than the person's usual state.
glossary.Bronchodilator: A drug that relaxes airway muscle and widens the airways.
glossary.Aspirin sensitivity: Worsening of asthma or nasal symptoms after taking aspirin or other NSAIDs.
glossary.Mucus plug: A thick lump of mucus that blocks a small airway.
glossary.Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis: An allergic reaction to the Aspergillus fungus in the airways, causing wheeze, eosinophilia and bronchiectasis.
glossary.Bronchiectasis: Permanent widening of the bronchi, causing chronic productive cough and repeated infections.
glossary.Bronchoconstriction: Narrowing of the airways due to tightening of the smooth muscle around them.
glossary.Eosinophilia: A raised number of eosinophils in the blood.
glossary.Sats: Oxygen saturation measured by a pulse oximeter on the finger.
glossary.Cyanosis: Blue discolouration of the lips or skin from low oxygen in the blood.
glossary.Bradycardia: A slow heart rate, under 60 beats per minute; in asthma a sign of impending arrest.
glossary.kPa: Kilopascals, the unit used for blood gas pressures such as PCO2.
glossary.Mechanical ventilation: A machine breathing for the patient through a tube in the airway.
glossary.Inflation pressure: The pressure the ventilator uses to push air into the lungs; high in near-fatal asthma due to narrow airways.
glossary.Spirometry: A breathing test measuring how much and how fast air can be blown out.
glossary.Salbutamol: A short-acting beta-2 agonist reliever inhaler that relaxes airway muscle within minutes.
glossary.Obstructive pattern: Spirometry showing low FEV1 and low FEV1/FVC ratio with normal FVC, meaning narrowed airways.
glossary.ULN: Upper limit of normal for a laboratory test.
glossary.Eosinophilic inflammation: Airway inflammation driven by eosinophils, typical of allergic asthma and responsive to steroids.
glossary.Biologics: Injected antibody drugs that block specific inflammatory pathways, used for severe asthma.
glossary.Serial peak flow: Repeated peak flow readings over days or weeks to show variability or a pattern.
glossary.Beclometasone dipropionate: An inhaled corticosteroid used as an asthma preventer.
glossary.Budesonide: An inhaled corticosteroid, often combined with formoterol in one inhaler.
glossary.PRN: Pro re nata: taken as needed.
glossary.Combination inhaler: One inhaler containing two drugs, such as a steroid and a long-acting bronchodilator.
glossary.Step-down: Reducing treatment once asthma has been well controlled for a sustained period.
glossary.Nocturnal symptoms: Symptoms at night, such as cough or waking breathless.
glossary.Nebulised: Given as a fine mist breathed in through a mask, driven by oxygen or air.
glossary.Prednisolone: An oral corticosteroid used to reduce airway inflammation in an acute attack.
glossary.Hydrocortisone: An IV corticosteroid used when the patient cannot take tablets, for example if vomiting.
glossary.ITU: Intensive therapy unit, for patients who need organ support such as ventilation.
glossary.Intubation: Passing a tube into the trachea to secure the airway and allow ventilation.
glossary.Histamine: A chemical released from mast cells that causes swelling, itch and airway narrowing.
glossary.Smooth muscle: Involuntary muscle, such as the muscle wrapped around the airways.
glossary.Mucosal oedema: Swelling of the airway lining due to fluid leaking from blood vessels.
glossary.Mucus hypersecretion: Excess production of mucus by the airway lining.
glossary.Eosinophilic infiltration: Eosinophils moving into and building up in a tissue such as the airway wall.
glossary.Airway remodelling: Long-term structural changes such as thickened walls and more muscle, causing fixed narrowing.
glossary.Airflow limitation: Reduced speed of air leaving the lungs because the airways are narrowed.
glossary.Beta-2 agonist: A drug that stimulates beta-2 receptors on airway muscle, causing it to relax.
glossary.Corticosteroids: Anti-inflammatory steroid drugs that switch off many inflammatory genes.
glossary.Cytokines: Signalling proteins released by immune cells that drive inflammation.
glossary.Hyperventilating: Breathing faster or deeper than needed, which blows off CO2 and lowers PCO2.
glossary.Calcium influx: Calcium entering a cell, which in smooth muscle triggers contraction.
glossary.Discharge criteria: Conditions a patient must meet before it is safe to send them home.
